Show it on both card faces — the narrow card in a lane and the wide summary card in the initiatives workflow — as a filled emerald circle with a white check, in the header beside the priority badge. One mark, and the card surface itself is left alone: a Done column is already tinted, and re-tinting every card in it would turn the most finished part of the board into the loudest. A large watermark was considered and rejected for the same reason — it would eat into the legibility the last task bought. Out of scope: changing what Done means, and any new stored field. DELIVERED: isComplete in the domain (rollupOf bucket === done), used by both card faces; a 16px emerald check in the card header, before the priority badge. Tested hardest on the negatives, including the 100%-but-not-done case that would make the stamp lie. Verified in the browser: only the card already in Done is stamped as seeded, moving one card stamps only that one, and the initiative gains its stamp only once all five leaves finish. 144 tests, was 143.
tasks.testStrategy: The risk is a false positive, not a false negative, so test the negatives hardest: a card in a Done column is stamped; a card in Backlog, Not Started or In Progress is not; an initiative whose leaves are all done is stamped; an initiative with one leaf still open is not, even when every other leaf is done and its percentage reads 100 — which is exactly the case `rollupOf` exists to get right. Then a browser check that the mark renders on both card shapes and on nothing else, and a screenshot of a board with a Done column and a mixed initiatives flow to confirm it reads as an affirmation rather than as another badge.

tasks.title: Set a card’s parent from its context menu, by pointing at an initiative
tasks.description: Connect a card to an initiative from the card itself. The context menu gains a “Set parent” option which puts the board into a pick mode; clicking an initiative there sets it as the card’s parent, and the card’s roll-up chip appears. Only a card connects to an initiative — an initiative is never the child of a card.
tasks.details: The item panel already has a Parent section with a select, so this is the same act done from the board — where the card and the initiative are both on screen and you can see what you are connecting to. A dropdown of every item by name is the fallback; pointing at the actual initiative is the thing a board can do that a list cannot. The mechanics are small: the menu gains an option, choosing it sets a mode in the store, and a click on an initiative in that mode calls the existing `setParent`. One parent, always — `setParent` replaces rather than appends, so picking a second initiative moves the card rather than giving it two, and the menu should offer to remove an existing parent as well as set one. The rule this rests on needs enforcing first, and it is what makes a loop impossible rather than merely unlikely: **an initiative is never the child of a card**. Connections run one way — a card rolls up to an initiative, and an initiative's parent is another initiative — so going down the tree the type can only fall from initiative to card, and nothing can ever be its own ancestor. That is a stronger and simpler answer than asking a picker to refuse a card's own subtree, and it belongs in the store, where every path already goes through it: `setParent` refuses an initiative whose parent is not an initiative. The panel's Parent select already excludes the item's own descendants — so it cannot make a loop either — but it offers every other item by name, including a card as an initiative's parent, so it is the half that is missing and should follow the same rule. The picker then needs no exclusion list at all — it offers initiatives, and a card cannot be a parent by construction. Only initiatives are offered, since a card rolls up to an outcome. The mode is the shape `boundaryId` already has — one id in the store, Escape to cancel, the board reads it — and a second mechanism for the same idea would be one too many. Feedback after picking: the card's roll-up chip, and the panel's Parent section if the card is open. Out of scope: changing what a parent means, setting parents for a whole selection at once, and the initiative side of the connection, which already has its own way in. DELIVERED: the rule lives in setParent, so every path gets it; the picker and the panel’s Parent select offer initiatives for the same reason. Pick mode dims everything that is not a choice and leaves the initiative lit; a click on a card does nothing and keeps the mode open. The initiative cards answer the pick from the initiatives workflow, which is where they are. Verified in the browser with real input. 150 tests, was 149.
tasks.testStrategy: The type rule first, because it is what makes the rest safe: an initiative whose parent would be a card is refused; an initiative under an initiative is allowed; a card under an initiative is allowed; a card under a card is allowed — the rule is about where initiatives may sit, not about how deep cards go. With that in place a cycle is unreachable, so the test asserts the rule rather than trying to enumerate loops: the store refuses the one edge that could start one. Then that setting a parent replaces rather than adds, and that removing one leaves the card a root. Then the interaction in the browser, with real input: the menu offers Set parent, choosing it puts the board in the mode, clicking an initiative sets the parent and the card's chip appears, clicking a card does nothing at all because a card cannot be a parent, and Escape leaves the parent exactly as it was. Run npm test.

tasks.title: A context menu for initiatives, and connecting a card from the initiative end
tasks.description: Initiative cards have no context menu at all. Give them one, and in it the same act task 64 added for cards but from the other end: pick a card and it becomes a child of this initiative — one edge, set from whichever end you happen to be looking at.
tasks.details: Task 64 let a card name the initiative it rolls up to, from the card. This is the same edge named from the initiative: you are looking at an outcome and you want to pull work under it, which is the moment the connection is actually in your head. Both ends set one decomposition edge, so both must go through `setParent` and neither may invent a second kind of link. The rule holds unchanged and is what makes it safe: a parent is always an initiative, so an initiative may only ever take children, never a parent that is a card. Initiative cards currently pass no `onContextMenu` at all, so the menu is new — reuse `CardMenu` rather than writing a second one, since most of what it offers (priority, assignees, size, dates, block, archive) applies to an initiative too, and the card-only entries are already guarded. The pick is the shape task 64 used: a mode in the store, a floating chip saying what to do, Escape to cancel, and the board resolving a click. The difference is which end is being chosen — there, an initiative among dimmed cards; here, a card among dimmed initiatives — so the mode needs a direction rather than a second mechanism, and the same `parentPickId` should grow one rather than being duplicated. Clicking anything that is not a valid choice does nothing and leaves the mode open, as before. Feedback after picking: the card appears as a child in the initiative's Hierarchy & Links, and its own roll-up chip appears on the card. DELIVERED: the wide card never wired onContextMenu, which is why initiatives had no menu at all; they have one now, reusing CardMenu. Connect a card… starts a mode that dims the initiatives and lights the cards — the same parentPick shape with a direction rather than a second mechanism. Verified in the browser with real input. 152 tests.
tasks.testStrategy: The rule first, unchanged and already tested: a parent is always an initiative, so connecting a card to an initiative is allowed and connecting an initiative to a card is not — assert the second is refused, because that is the one this feature makes easy to attempt from the wrong end. Then that both directions produce exactly one decomposition edge: connecting from the initiative and then from the card names the same edge, not two. Then the interaction in the browser with real input: an initiative has a context menu, the connect option puts the board in a pick mode, clicking a card sets the parent and closes the mode, clicking an initiative does nothing and keeps it open, and Escape leaves the graph exactly as it was. Run npm test.

tasks.title: Connect a team initiative to a management one, from a Program board
tasks.description: A Program board shows each linked board as a band, and a band is read-only today — not by policy but because the context menu has nowhere to render there. Allow the one act that belongs on this surface: a team initiative in a band rolling up to a management initiative on the board itself.
tasks.details: Measured rather than assumed: on a Program board a right-click opens nothing at all. The reason is structural — `CardMenu` is rendered by `BoardCanvas`, and an aggregating board does not render `BoardCanvas`, so the menu has nowhere to appear. The same is true of the floating chip the pick mode shows. So the first move is to hoist the menu and the chip out of the cards canvas into something both surfaces mount, rather than rendering a second menu for aggregation. The band already passes `boardId`, and the pick already sets a parent through `setParent`, which is board-agnostic — so the connection itself needs nothing new. What it needs is a narrower set of choices: the pick must offer only the initiatives *on the board being viewed*, or a band could parent another band and the act stops being the flight-level one. `initiativeCellOf(id, boardId, graph)` already answers that — it is undefined for an item that is not on that board — so the guard is a lookup rather than a new rule. Drag stays off the bands, deliberately: a drag is a move, and moving another board's initiative from here edits a board you are not looking at. Its section restriction would be the only guard, and a lens should not move things. Out of scope: making bands editable in general, and the reverse act of linking from the management end, which the item panel already offers. PARTLY DELIVERED: CardMenu and the pick chips moved into an Overlays host mounted by App, so an aggregating board has them — verified that a band initiative opens a menu offering Set parent and that the chip appears. The scoping rule is in too, with viewedBoardId so a band knows which board is being looked at rather than assuming its own. REMAINING, and unverified: clicking a management initiative completing the connection, and clicking another band initiative being refused. The probe closed the mode on a band click, which the guard should have prevented, and there was no room left to find the real click path. DELIVERED: CardMenu and the pick chips moved into an Overlays host mounted by App, so an aggregating board has them; the choices are the initiatives on the board being viewed, with viewedBoardId so a band knows which board that is. The guard originally used initiativeCellOf, which falls back to a section first cell and so answered yes for another board entirely — it checks the placement now. Verified on a Program board: band initiatives dim to 0.4 while the board own stay at 1, a band click leaves the graph unchanged and the mode open, and a management click sets the parent and closes it. 151 tests.
tasks.testStrategy: The scoping rule first, because it is the whole of the new behaviour: the pick offers the initiatives on the board being viewed and not the band's, so a team initiative can be connected to a management one and two band initiatives cannot be connected to each other. Then that the act produces one decomposition edge and that the rule still holds from this surface — a parent is always an initiative. Then the interaction in the browser with real input: on a Program board a band's initiative has a context menu, the option puts the board in a pick mode with the chip visible, clicking a management initiative sets the parent and closes the mode, clicking another band's initiative does nothing and leaves it open, and Escape leaves the graph unchanged. Run npm test.

tasks.title: Bug: a card's drop shadow outlives the drop and takes up space on the board
tasks.description: After dropping a card, the insertion-gap placeholder stays in the lane — above the dropped card, occupying a slot — until the next drag begins.
tasks.details: Reported with a screenshot: after dropping Build signup form into a DONE column, the shadow placeholder sits above it and the card reads as moved below the shadow. ROOT CAUSE: BoardCanvas holds the gap in its own state (dropAt, set by onMove) and nothing ever clears it — onDrop resolves the gap and moves the card but never setDropAt(null), and there is no cleanup when the lift ends. The lane then renders at={ctx.drag.laneId === lane.id ? ctx.drag.index : null} with no guard on a lift being live, so once the gesture is over (lift null, draggingId null, the dropped card back in the list) the placeholder still renders at that index in that lane — above the card that now occupies the slot. It looks intermittent but it is every drop: it heals only when the next drag's first onMove overwrites dropAt. FIX SHAPE: gate the drag preview on the gesture being live — the lifting flag (lift !== null) already exists in BoardCanvas, so ctx.drag's laneId/index should read null when it is not — and clear dropAt in onDrop for hygiene. BoardSummary's dropCell has the same never-cleared shape and needs the same gate, otherwise fixing cards leaves the same latent bug in the initiatives workflow. DELIVERED: the gap is live only while a card is in the air \u2014 BoardCanvas gates its drag preview on the gesture (lifting), onDrop clears dropAt, and BoardSummary keeps the same rule (previewCell) so the fix is one idea in both workflows. Verified with real input (Input.dispatchMouseEvent): placeholder present during a held cross-lane drag, zero placeholders anywhere after release, the card moved and moved back, twice.
tasks.testStrategy: Browser probe with real input (Input.dispatchMouseEvent — synthetic DragEvents bypass the machinery): press a card, move it over a lane gap, release, then assert no [data-drop-placeholder] remains anywhere in the document, and that the landed lane's children are exactly its cards with no extra block. Repeat for a cross-lane move and a drop back into the origin lane.

tasks.title: Bug: initiative drags never show a drop target, where cards show the gap they would land in
tasks.description: Dragging an initiative gives no live drop feedback at all — no placeholder in the target cell — while a dragged card shows the insertion gap following the pointer.
tasks.details: Reported alongside the stale-card-shadow bug. ROOT CAUSE: a stale closure, not a missing render. BoardSummary's drag callback reads the dragged item as lift?.itemId — but useCardLift registers its pointermove listener once, at pointerdown, with the closure from that render, and never re-registers; lift only becomes non-null DURING the first move. So lift?.itemId is null for the entire drag, cellUnder cannot resolve the dragged initiative's own cell (here = undefined) and bails, dropCell never sets, and the placeholder in Cell never renders. The drop itself still lands correctly because onDrop receives itemId as a parameter rather than reading lift — which is exactly why this survived: the one path that works hides the one that does not. Cards were immune by accident: BoardCanvas's gapUnder reads the DOM (elementFromPoint, data-card-id), no React state, so its onMove closure going stale costs it nothing. FIX SHAPE: useCardLift already knows the itemId — pass it to onMove(itemId, x, y) so no callback ever reads lift through a stale closure; BoardCanvas's onMove ignores the extra argument. DESIGN CONSTRAINT when fixing: initiative cells have no order — a per-position gap inside a cell would be meaningless, so the intended feedback is the cell-level shadow (the placeholder at the top of the target cell, which already exists in Cell behind isTarget), not a card-style insertion gap. Dragging within an initiative's own cell deliberately shows nothing (there is no within-cell reorder to preview); decide whether that silence is right or whether the origin cell should say 'stays here'. DELIVERED: useCardLift hands the dragged item\u2019s id to onMove(itemId, x, y) \u2014 the listener is registered once at pointerdown, so no callback may read lift through its closure; BoardSummary\u2019s cellUnder now takes the id as a parameter and the target cell lights during the drag. The cell-level shadow stays the design (cells have no order); within the origin cell nothing shows, as before. Verified end to end on a Program board after splitting a section in edit mode and saving: held over the sibling cell the target renders the placeholder BEFORE release; release moves the initiative and leaves nothing; held over another section\u2019s cell nothing lights and nothing moves. FOLLOW-UP FIX, reported after delivery with a screenshot: in a split section the space above a sub-lane rendered the drop shadow even though the store refuses drops there \u2014 a container\u2019s own body answers closest([data-cell-id]) too, and cellUnder never asked whether the hit was a leaf. cellUnder now requires one, so a shadow only stands where a drop would be accepted; and a leaf cell now marks its whole widget (header included) so pointing at a row\u2019s header bar targets that row, which previously resolved to the container and did nothing. Verified on a rows-split section: held over the strip above Row 1, nothing lights while the card is in the air; Row 2\u2019s body shows exactly one placeholder; releases move correctly and leave nothing; the Row 1 header previews and accepts for Row 1.
tasks.testStrategy: Browser probe with real input: press an initiative, move it over another cell of its own section, and assert the target cell renders [data-drop-placeholder] BEFORE release (during pointermove); assert it is gone after release. Also assert a move over a different section's cell and over the origin cell show nothing, and that the drop still moves the initiative.

tasks.title: Aging and staleness: time-in-column on cards, a stale filter, and column age on the dashboard
tasks.description: Surface how long work has been sitting where it is — derived from laneEnteredAt, never stored, never blocking.
tasks.details: Competitor basis: LeanKit's staleness filter and card/board health; Businessmap's aging-work analytics. Flowline already stores laneEnteredAt on every placement and the domain has ageDays \u2014 the data exists, nothing new is recorded. Three surfaces, all derived at render: (1) time-in-column on cards, quiet until it matters \u2014 a subtle cue that appears only past a threshold, so the board stays calm and the old work speaks up; (2) a stale filter in the existing filter panel (is this card older than N days in its current column) with a sensible default \u2014 pick one in build, say 7 days \u2014 composing with the other filters; (3) per-column age on the management dashboard \u2014 oldest and median time-in-column per column, so a stuck column is a number before it is a feeling. CONSTRAINTS: nothing is auto-moved, nothing is auto-flagged, no notifications \u2014 time-respecting means the facts are always visible and never nag; age is read from placements, never written onto items.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit tests for the staleness predicate including the boundary (a card exactly N days old), and for the dashboard column-age computation (oldest/median across a lane's placements). Filter integration: stale composes with blocked/assignee/type filters. Browser probe: a seeded old placement shows the aging cue, the filter isolates it, and a fresh placement shows nothing.

tasks.title: Filter updates: text search, saved filters, due-soon status, unassigned as an assignee option
tasks.description: Four additions to the card filter panel, one control per concept.
tasks.details: (1) TEXT SEARCH as a filter criterion \u2014 there is a separate top-bar search today; the filter panel gains a text field over title/description, and the two must compose rather than duplicate: decide in build whether search moves into filters entirely or the two AND together. (2) SAVED FILTERS \u2014 named, persisted filter sets (Windshift's saved searches): save the current filters under a name, re-apply from the panel. This is the one persisted piece \u2014 persist version bump and a migrate backfill, and coordinate with any other pending bump so only one migration lands. (3) DUE SOON as a status option \u2014 a date-bucket alongside blocked and overdue: targetEndDate within the next N days and not resolved. Pick N in build (a week is the obvious default) and pin the boundary in a test. (4) UNASSIGNED as an assignee option \u2014 the separate unassigned toggle becomes a pseudo-entry in the assignee filter: one concept, one control, composable with picked assignees. CONSTRAINTS: filters are view state and never persisted \u2014 saved filters are the deliberate exception; filters are explicit \u2014 nothing is hidden by default; narrowing what you see never changes what a column carries.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit tests per predicate: due-soon boundary (end date today+N-1 in, today+N+1 out), unassigned composing with explicit assignee ids, text search over title and description case-insensitively. Saved filters: round-trip through migratePersisted with a pre-bump payload, and that applying one leaves no residue when cleared. Browser probe: each filter isolates seeded cards; a saved filter survives a reload.

tasks.title: Board legend and board information: a description field and a panel that explains this board
tasks.description: A panel that brings a newcomer from zero to reading the board: what it is, what the colours mean, where the policies live.
tasks.details: Competitor basis: LeanKit's board legend and lane policies; the description field is the board's own voice. Two parts. (1) A DESCRIPTION FIELD on the board \u2014 persisted, so a persist version bump and a migrate that backfills an empty string; edited from board settings, shown in the legend and plausibly in the workspace. (2) A LEGEND PANEL that explains this board to someone who just arrived, all of it derived from the live graph so it cannot drift: the description; card types with their colours (types are workspace-wide); the four stages and what they mean on this workflow; lane policies gathered in one place (the text already exists per lane \u2014 this surfaces it); what a WIP limit means here (visual only, never blocks); what band this board is and what that lens shows. Any other useful facts are welcome if derived \u2014 counts per column, dependency and blocked counts \u2014 but nothing time-stamped: last-updated was explicitly cut and stays cut. Where the panel lives (board header button, settings, or an info affordance) is a build decision.
tasks.testStrategy: migratePersisted backfills description on a pre-bump payload and preserves an existing one. The legend renders from the graph: renaming a type or editing a policy changes the legend without a second edit. Browser probe: the panel opens from a board, shows the live types/colours/policies, and the description round-trips through a reload.

tasks.title: CSV export: the board and the dashboard as downloaded files
tasks.description: Local-first means the data is yours: one explicit action produces a CSV.
tasks.details: Export the current board's cards as CSV \u2014 ref, title, type, column (its lane), assignees, blocked and reason, target dates, parent \u2014 and the management dashboard's initiative rows in a second shape. Generated client-side and downloaded directly: no server exists and none is needed. The serialiser must quote properly \u2014 titles with commas, quotes and newlines are the normal case, not the edge case. One explicit action per export; import is out of scope for this slice. Competitor basis: LeanKit and Windshift both export; for Flowline it is the cheapest possible expression of data ownership.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit tests for the serialiser: embedded commas, double quotes, newlines, and unicode titles round-trip through a standard CSV parse; empty lanes produce headers only. Browser probe: the download fires with the expected row count matching the board's cards.

tasks.title: My work across boards: everything assigned to me, wherever it lives
tasks.description: A view over the graph: all of the current user's assigned work across every board, with its board and cell context.
tasks.details: Competitor basis: LeanKit's My Cards, Businessmap's My Queue, Windshift's personal view \u2014 all three converge here, and Flowline's graph makes it cheap: assignments are on items, placements say where each sits. The query: every item whose assignees include the current user, joined with its placements, grouped by board (and plausibly by urgency \u2014 overdue and due-soon first, reusing the filters work). Each entry shows its board and cell context so the answer to \u2018where is this?’ is on the card; clicking opens the item panel. SURFACE: a nav tab alongside Board/Dashboard/Timeline/Archive, or a panel \u2014 decide in build against the tabs model; the nav is tabs now and a new tab must earn its place. CONSTRAINTS: fully derived \u2014 no my-work flag, no second placement record; moves still happen on boards, this view opens work rather than relocating it; assignment reads the local users, so it is per-browser by nature.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit test the cross-board query: an item assigned to the user on two boards appears twice with the right placement contexts; unassigned and other-user items never appear. Browser probe: seeded assignments on two boards both appear, grouped sensibly, and clicking one opens the item panel.

tasks.title: Record the moved event: an item's lane changes belong in its history
tasks.description: Extend the item log with a `moved` event, written on every lane change, so a card carries its journey and not just its current cell. The prerequisite task 59 already assumes, and what makes a register auditable.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit-test that `moveCard` and `moveInitiative` append a `moved` entry naming from/to, that a same-cell reorder writes nothing, and that the split/remove rehoming writes one with its reason. Unit-test that an item persisted without any log still loads and renders (the Activity tab's ‘No events yet.’ path). Over CDP: drag a card between cells and confirm the entry appears in the Activity tab with the right from/to; split the column it sits in and confirm the entry explains the move. Run npm test and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: Duplicate a card: the “copy me” template for a consistently-shaped record
tasks.description: An explicit Duplicate action on a card that produces a fresh item with the same type, size, description and checklist (reset to undone), titled “… copy”, and none of the original's state.
tasks.details:
Basis: the LeanKit register practice keeps a “Copy me!” template card in a Template cell of the board, so every new risk is created with the same shape and the same prompts. Flowline has `duplicateLane` and `duplicateBoard` — structure, not work — and no way to copy a card. A template *entity* is not needed and would be a second kind of design alongside `BoardTemplate`; a card you copy is the same idea with nothing new to persist.

What the copy carries: title `<title> copy`, `typeId`, `size`, `description`, and the checklist with **fresh entry ids and `done: false`** — a copied checklist is a fresh set of steps, never a set already ticked. Fresh `id`, `createdAt`, and `log: [logEntry('created')]`.

What it deliberately does not carry: `assignees`, `priority`, `blocked` / `blockedReason`, `targetStartDate` / `targetEndDate`, `resolvedAt`, `lastMoveReason`, `archived` — these are judgements about *that* card; and no placement, no parent edge, no links, no dependency edges. A copy is a new card with none of the original's commitments.

Where it lands — SETTLE THIS: invoked from a board (card context menu, item panel opened from a board), the copy lands in the same cell, directly below the original, reusing `nextRank` / the same placement path a new card takes so lane ordering stays clean. Offered from a surface with no cell context (search, archive, My work) it should be refused rather than guessed — or land via `defaultDropLane`; pick one and say so in the UI (a disabled action explains itself).

Notes: no persist version bump — this mints a normal `Item`, no new fields. The refused-with-reason path must not half-create: one `addItem`-shaped store action, so a failure leaves nothing behind. `buildRefs` is derived from the items array, so the copy takes the next ordinal for its type prefix; its instability (a deletion renumbers later items) is the subject of a separate idea, not fixed here. Also wire the same action into wherever a card's context menu already lives so the affordance is not board-canvas-only.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit-test the store action: a copy is a distinct item with a fresh id, the checklist is copied with fresh ids and everything undone, and assignees / dates / priority / blocked / parent / links / placements are all absent; and that copying a card with no checklist yields none. Over CDP: duplicate a card carrying a fully-ticked checklist and confirm the copy reads “… copy”, sits directly below the original, has an unticked checklist, no assignees and an Activity tab holding only its creation; confirm the action is absent or refused where no cell is known. Run npm test and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: Initiative types: a board's own label on an initiative, with a None that cannot be removed
tasks.description: Boards define their own initiative types — a name and a colour that style and organise initiatives, called “Kind” in the UI — with None always available, mandatory and unremovable, every kind behaving identically, and a kind filter scoped to the board's initiatives flow.
tasks.details:
Basis: cards already have a **type** — a label and a colour that says what kind of work something is, with a per-board *default* — and the initiatives workflow has nothing of the kind, so a portfolio board reads a flat list of initiatives with no way to say "this one is a bet, that one is a programme". This adds the same idea one level up: an **initiative type** is a styling option on an initiative and a way to organise different kinds of them, and **every kind behaves identically** — no lifecycle, no columns, no WIP, no rollup, no health, no metrics. That is the rule the model already states for types: "Issue types are labels + colour. Columns come from a board's lane tree, never from the type."

Prior art (Businessmap, *Overview of the Initiative Properties* / *What Is an Initiative and How Does it Work*): their initiatives carry a **Type** property — "hover over the icon to see the current initiative type; click once to change the type" — changed inline from the card or from the initiative's context menu, and an initiative's icons "appear only when a corresponding property value is set", so an unset property renders as nothing at all. That is this feature, and it is worth taking two things from it: the *inline* change (the chip itself opening the picker is better than a trip to the panel) and the "set means visible, unset means absent" convention, which is what None already means here. The deliberate deviation: they use one type vocabulary for cards and initiatives alike, which we cannot do — the `IssueType` named *Initiative* is reserved and means something else — so this is a second, initiative-only vocabulary with a mandatory None.

**Settled by the product owner, so the implementation does not re-decide it:**
- **Per board, not workspace-wide.** v27 deleted per-board card-type *subsets* on purpose ("a board either has a type, which is to say everyone does, or the type does not exist"), so following it was the obvious move. The reason not to: an initiative type is **management vocabulary about a board's own outcomes** — a portfolio board says *Bet / Programme / Experiment*, a team board may have none at all — while a card type is the *work* vocabulary that everyone doing that work shares. So `Board.initiativeTypes?: InitiativeType[]`, with the asymmetry against card types deliberate and commented where it is read. Two boards may each have a "Bet" and they are different types: no cross-board registry, no sharing, no global vocabulary.
- **The UI says "Kind".** In the item panel "Type" already means the reserved Initiative type ("Type is fixed. An initiative is defined by the Initiative type…"), so the new control is **Kind** — on the chip, in the panel, in board settings, and as the CSV column header. The model keeps `InitiativeType` / `initiativeTypeId`, matching the model's own word for `IssueType`; that the two words differ is deliberate and wants a line of comment so nobody "fixes" it later.
- **Removing a kind that is in use is refused, and says how many carry it.** The house pattern — refused rather than corrected, never a silent blanking: the board reports "3 initiatives still carry this" and the person clears those first. Note that `removeIssueType` today silently filters and leaves items pointing at nothing, which is the precedent *not* to copy.
- **The "+ Initiative" button always creates a plain one.** One click to create, exactly as today; the kind is set in the panel afterwards, which keeps creating separate from classifying.
- **The kind is also a filter — scoped to the board's initiatives flow.** The filter panel is cards-only and the initiatives flow reads nothing today, so a kind filter needs a home and a scope. This slice puts it in the initiatives workflow's header (the cards workflow's own Filters button is the model) and has it narrow *which initiatives the flow shows*. It is view state like every other filter — never persisted, and the saved-preset system stays card filters only. It does **not** touch the cards workflow, or the dashboard, timeline or strategy map: those read the same initiatives but they are not the board, and one control changing four surfaces is a bigger idea than a label. (If it should narrow the cards beneath a kind as well, that is the one thing to say so before this is built.)

**Do not overload `IssueType`.** The `IssueType` named *Initiative* is reserved: it is what makes an item an initiative at all, `initiativeTypeId` / `isReservedType` / `canRetype` read it, and the initiatives workflow is built on it. An initiative kind is a second, orthogonal label *on top of* that. So `Item.typeId` keeps meaning what it means and the new field is separate and named so the two cannot be confused: `Item.initiativeTypeId`, documented against `typeId`, with `InitiativeType { id; name; color }` mirroring `IssueType`'s shape so the chip, `chipColors` and the contrast guard are reused rather than reinvented.

**None is the absence of a value, not an entry in a list.** `initiativeTypeId === undefined` *is* None. That is what makes the requirement structural instead of a UI rule: there is no "none" row anyone can delete, an initiative with no kind reads as None everywhere by construction, and old persisted items read as None with no backfill. A board's list may be empty and every picker still has exactly one option — None, always first.

**Resolving a kind across boards.** An initiative can be placed on more than one board — a decomposition crosses boards, and a management board and a team board may both hold the same initiative — while the field is item-level, so a kind defined on one board can be read on another. Resolve by id across every board's list (one small helper), render the chip from the definition wherever it is found, and render **nothing** rather than a raw id when the definition is gone (a board deleted with items on it). Never copy the name and colour onto the item: a kind renamed must rename everywhere at once, the rule lanes and card types already follow. Task 82 (tags) has the same wrinkle and states the same rule.

Rules the **model** enforces, not only the UI (the house pattern): only an initiative can carry one, so setting `initiativeTypeId` on a card is refused by the store rather than merely hidden by the panel; an initiative's `typeId` stays the reserved Initiative type and a card's stays a card type (`canRetype` already says so), so the new field never becomes a way around it; a board's list cannot contain an entry that stands for None and nothing can remove None; and renaming or recolouring a kind in use is fine and shows everywhere at once, the rule lanes and card types already follow.

Where it surfaces (this slice): the initiative's card face, as a chip beside the type chip, in its own colour (`chipColors`, so contrast holds on every ground) and clickable to change it, as Businessmap's is; the item panel, as a **Kind** control where the fixed-type paragraph is today — that paragraph must stay, because it explains that the *Initiative* type is fixed, and the new control sits beside it rather than instead of it; the initiatives workflow's header, as the kind filter; board settings, as a section to add, rename, recolour and remove, next to the card-type picker but clearly distinct from it (that section's label already says "Card types on this board" while v27 made it a *default* picker — fix that copy while here); and the dashboard's CSV export, whose rows are initiatives. The board export stays cards-only, because that is what it exports.

Persistence: both fields are optional, so old state reads as None and no list — **no version bump and no migrate**, which an optional field does not need. Export/import carries boards and items wholesale, so `WORKSPACE_KEYS` is unchanged. `duplicateBoard` copies a board's kinds with the rest of its design; a `BoardTemplate` does **not** carry them, because a template designs a flow and v27 settled that it is not a shortlist of types.

Non-goals: no lifecycle, state or transition of any kind; no columns, sections, cells or WIP from a kind; no permissions; no cross-board sharing or registry; and no effect on rollup, health, dependencies, flow metrics, search or the timeline. The kind filter narrows *what the initiatives flow shows* and nothing else — counts read the column, as everywhere.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit-test the None rule (an item with no `initiativeTypeId` reads as None; a board's list has no None entry to delete, and an empty list still offers exactly one option); add, rename, recolour and remove a board's own kind; removing one that is in use is refused and says how many carry it; setting one on a card is refused; and `canRetype` still holds with the field in place, so an initiative stays an initiative and a card stays a card. **Parity as a test rather than a claim**: for one initiative, assert its rollup bucket, its lane's card count, its health flags, its dependency state and the board's flow numbers are identical with and without a kind set. **The filter's scope, also as a test**: with a kind selected, the initiatives flow shows fewer initiatives while the cards workflow, every lane count, the dashboard, the timeline and the strategy map are unchanged; the filter is not persisted and does not appear in the saved presets. Persistence: a board with kinds round-trips through `persistedSlice` / `migrateState`; an old board without the field loads with none; `duplicateBoard` carries them and `templateFromBoard` does not. Over CDP: set a kind on an initiative and see the chip on the card face and in the panel; filter the initiatives flow by it and watch the flow narrow while the board's counts and health do not move; remove the kind and watch the chip go; confirm None is always in the picker and cannot be removed. Run `npm test` and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: Cumulative size, and the two warnings that read it
tasks.description: Derive an initiative's cumulative size — the sizes of the leaf work below it, an unsized leaf counting as 1 — and raise two health warnings from it: work below due after the initiative, and work below bigger than the initiative says it is.
tasks.details:
Basis: Businessmap's initiative warnings (an exclamation mark on the initiative) fire in exactly two cases — "if you have an initiative scheduled with a particular deadline, but one or more of its child cards deadline is set to end later", and "if the total size of your child cards at the lowest level in the hierarchy exceeds the size of the Initiative". Their cumulative size is the sum of the child cards' sizes through the hierarchy, and an unset size counts as 1.

Both are arithmetic over things we already keep: `Item.size`, the decomposition, and `targetEndDate`. `rollupOf` already walks the leaves for counts, so this is a `size` beside `total`/`done`, and the two warnings are two more flags in the health module (task 10) — which is the same mechanism Businessmap's exclamation mark is, and ours comes with the reason attached.

Shape: `Rollup.size` (the sum below, unsized leaves as 1) and `Rollup.ownSize` (the initiative's own `size`, when set), then `oversized` ("the work below is 34, this initiative says 21") and `outlasted` ("a card below is due after this initiative is") as watch-level flags. Per the house rule they are surfaced, never enforced: no block, no auto-correction, and an initiative with no work below raises neither.

Worth deciding while here: whether the cumulative size shows on the initiative's card face (Businessmap shows it in a dedicated field) or only in the panel and the flags' tooltips.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit-test the sum: through a hierarchy of two levels, unsized leaves counting as 1, an initiative with no work below reading 0, and an initiative's own size staying its own. Test both flags raised and cleared (the deadline moved earlier, the size raised to cover the work), that neither fires on an initiative with nothing below, and that neither changes a rollup bucket or a lane count. Over CDP: an initiative with an oversized child shows the flag and its why. Run npm test and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: Progress by size, not by counting leaves
tasks.description: Weight an initiative's progress by the size of the work below it, so finishing a 13-point epic moves the number more than finishing a 2-point task.
tasks.details:
Basis: Businessmap's progress is "cumulative size of all completed child cards / cumulative size of all child cards", unsized cards counting as 1 — and their worked example is the argument: a Timeline initiative read 69% rather than 50% when one of its two projects finished, because the marketing cards were bigger than the sales ones. Counting leaves treats a 13 beside a 2 as two equal pieces of work.

Ours is `Rollup.percent = done / countable leaves`, blind to size. Weighting it is a small change to a core derivation, and it is *coherent* rather than disruptive: the extremes do not move (every committed leaf done is still 100%, none is still 0%), so only the middle of a portfolio reads differently — and the *bucket* must stay exactly as it is, because it reads the leaves' stages and not the percentage. That is the line to hold: a size-weighted number never moves a card's status.

SETTLE THIS: replace `percent`, or add a second number. Recommendation: **replace it, keep the counts beside it** — the dashboard already prints "1 of 5 done · 3 active", so nothing is lost, and two percentages of the same thing on one card would be the drift this model exists to avoid. The existing rule that Backlog leaves are excluded from the denominator stays (Businessmap has no equivalent, and it is the one that keeps a partly-planned initiative from reading 0%), as does "100% is not the same as done" — an initiative with every committed leaf finished and one still unplanned reads 100% and is not complete.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit-test the weighting: equal sizes match the old count exactly (the backwards-compatible case), one big leaf dominates several small ones, unsized leaves count as 1, Backlog leaves stay out of the denominator, all-done is 100 and none-done is 0, and the 100%-but-not-done case still reads 100% while its bucket stays not-done. Assert the bucket is identical with and without sizes set. Over CDP: the card's percentage and the dashboard's agree after a leaf moves. Run npm test and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: Planned dates that mean something: a delay band, and inheritance from the work below
tasks.description: Replace the binary overdue marker with a delay band — how far past a planned window the work is, as a percentage — and let an initiative's planned dates be read from its children instead of typed in.
tasks.details:
Basis: Businessmap bands delay against the planned duration — yellow under 15%, orange 15–30%, red at 30% or more — colours the initiative's edge (a late *start* on the left, a late *end* on the right) and names the percentage on hover; with no planned end date, any delay is red. They also let a parent's planned start and end inherit from its children's.

Ours is binary: `isOverdue` is "the target end date is past and it isn't resolved", which cannot tell a week late from a quarter late — and every initiative's window is typed in by hand even when its work already knows when it will run. Both halves are derivable from what we keep (`targetStartDate`, `targetEndDate`, `resolvedAt`, and the placements' arrival stamps), which is the shape this app prefers: nothing to maintain, nothing invented.

First half: a delay band per planned date — the late start and the late end separately, each as a percentage of the planned duration, in the same three bands, surfaced where the overdue marker is today (the dashboard's target column, the card's date chip, the timeline's bar) with the percentage in the tooltip. Keep it a read: no auto-correction, and never a date written onto an item.

Second half: an initiative whose own dates are unset reads the earliest start and the latest end of the work below it — explicitly *derived*, shown as inherited rather than owned, so nothing is written to the item and clearing the work's dates empties it again. An initiative that has its own dates keeps them.

Non-goals: milestones (Businessmap's, a real feature and its own slice), actual start/end as *stored* fields (ours are derivations already: `resolvedAt`, and the first commit in the log), and any notion of a schedule that blocks.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit-test the band: nothing late reads no band; a late start and a late end are separate; under 15%, 15–30% and over 30% land where they should; a missing planned end makes any delay red (their rule, and the honest one); and a resolved item is never late. Unit-test inheritance: an initiative with no dates of its own reads its children's earliest start and latest end, one with its own keeps them, an initiative with no dated work below inherits nothing, and the derived dates are never written to the item. Over CDP: the band appears, its tooltip names the percentage, and the dashboard and the card agree. Run npm test and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: A forecast you can defend: when will this finish, from the history
tasks.description: Answer "when will this finish?" from the movement history: the distribution of how long comparable work actually took, sampled across the work below an initiative, reported as a range rather than a date.
tasks.details:
Basis: Businessmap's Forecast / "What if analysis" takes an initiative's child cards, finds similar cards that were finished in the past, runs thousands of samples and reports Optimistic / Realistic / Pessimistic / Very Pessimistic in days. Task 59 deliberately left Monte Carlo forecasting out of the flow view; this is that slice, and it is only possible now because the history exists — task 74 records every move, task 59 derives `leadTimes` and `cycleTimes`, so the distribution a sample would draw from is already computed and already on screen.

Shape: per initiative, sample the remaining leaves' cycle times from the observed distribution (recent deliveries, the same board's work, the same size band when there is one), sum the samples, and report percentiles — p50, p85, p95 — as a *range in days*, with the sample size and the history's start date beside it, because a range built on four deliveries is not the same claim as one built on forty.

The house rules apply with force here: it is a **projection, never a promise** — no target is stored, nothing is written onto an item, and no date appears on the timeline from it. A forecast with too little history says so rather than guessing, which is the same rule as an unknown card age. And the sampling must be **seeded**, so the same board and the same history give the same answer twice — a number that moves when you reload it is not a number anyone can use.

Where it belongs: the initiative's panel first (a Forecast section, read-only), and the Flow view as a secondary reading. Not on the card face.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit-test the sampler over synthetic histories: a seeded run is reproducible; percentiles come back ordered and inside the observed range; an initiative with no comparable history reports nothing rather than a guess; an initiative with every leaf delivered reports no remaining work; and nothing is written to any item (assert the state is byte-identical after a forecast). Over CDP: an initiative with enough history shows a range, one without says why not. Run npm test and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: An initiative with nothing below it can be moved between sections
tasks.description: Fix `moveInitiative` refusing to move a childless initiative to another section, which contradicts the model's own rule that a leaf's status comes from its column's stage.
tasks.details:
Found while reading Businessmap's initiative article, which states the case plainly: "If an initiative does not have any linked child cards, it can be moved freely between all the sections of the workflow manually." Ours cannot. Verified against the demo: `init-data-quality` (Data quality guardrails, no work below, sitting in Backlog) refuses a move to Not Started.

The cause is circular. `moveInitiative` refuses unless `effectiveStage(target) === rollupOf(itemId).bucket`, and for an initiative with no descendants `rollupOf` reads *the item's own placement* — so the check compares the destination against the place it is trying to leave, and the answer is always no. The move is not just refused, it is invisible: a drag simply does not move anything.

That contradicts the model as documented: "A leaf's status comes from its column's stage" — an initiative with nothing under it *is* a leaf, so its status is whatever section it sits in, and the section is the only fact there is. Which is also how a portfolio actually works: you commit to a bet, then break it down; today the second step is mandatory before the first.

Fix: skip the bucket check when the initiative has no descendants (`descendants(itemId, graph).length === 0`), and leave it in place for every other initiative — the derived-section rule is right for work that exists. Worth a test on both sides so the carve-out cannot widen: a childless initiative moves between sections and *within* one, and an initiative with work still refuses a cross-section move. Also worth deciding: should the refusal say so on screen? Today a refused drag is silent, which is the one thing the house rules dislike.
tasks.testStrategy: Store test: an initiative with no descendants moves from Backlog to Not Started and back; one with work below still refuses a cross-section move and still allows a cell move inside its own section; and moving a childless initiative never writes a moved entry with a wrong stage. Over CDP: drag the demo's unplanned initiative to another section and watch it land, then confirm the rollup, health and counts around it are unchanged. Run npm test and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: Tags: a board's own labels on cards and initiatives
tasks.description: Boards define their own tags — a name and a colour — and any card or initiative can carry several, as labels for finding work rather than a status.
tasks.details:
Basis: Businessmap's initiatives carry a **Tag** property beside their Type ("hover over the icon to see the tag name; click once to change the tag"), and the two are different concepts there and here: a type says *what kind of thing this is* — one per item, from a board's short list — while a tag says *what this is about* — several, added freely. Theirs is one tag per item; ours is several, which is the plural reading of the request and the more useful one. **SETTLE THIS** and record the answer: several tags per item is the shape below, and if it should be one, say so before this is built, because the field and the chips are different.

**Where the list lives: per board.** `Board.tags?: Tag[]` with `Tag { id; name; color }` mirroring `IssueType`'s shape, so the chip, `chipColors` and the contrast guard are reused rather than reinvented; applied as `Item.tagIds?: string[]`, so an item carries ids and never a copy. This is the same call task 76 makes for initiative kinds and for the same reason — a tag is a board's own vocabulary for its own work (a team board's "tech-debt" means nothing on a portfolio board) — and v27's argument against per-board card-type *subsets* does not apply, because that was a shortlist of the workspace's types, not a board's own labels. No cross-board registry, no sharing: two boards may each have a "security" and they are different tags.

**No mandatory None.** An empty set *is* the empty state — unlike an initiative's kind, which needed a default option in a picker because a single choice always has to resolve to something. A tag set is a set: none, one or several, and "none" is not a row anyone can delete because it is not a row.

**Resolving a tag across boards — the wrinkle worth stating once.** An item can be placed on more than one board (a decomposition crosses boards; a management board and a team board may both hold the same initiative) while the field is item-level, so a tag defined on one board can be read on another. Resolve by id across every board's list, render the chip from the definition wherever it is found, and render **nothing** — never a raw id — when the definition is gone, which can happen when a board is deleted while items placed on it live on. Never copy the name and colour onto the item: a tag renamed must rename everywhere at once, the rule lanes, card types and initiative kinds all follow.

Rules the **model** enforces, not only the UI (the house pattern): a tag id must belong to a board's list at the moment it is applied, and the picker offers that board's tags only; the same tag cannot be applied twice; and **removing a tag that is in use is refused, and says how many carry it** — the answer settled for initiative kinds, and the opposite of `removeIssueType`, which silently filters and leaves items pointing at nothing.

**Behaviour parity, and the one thing that reads them.** Tags change nothing: no lifecycle, no rollup, no WIP, no health, no metrics, no sections, no dependencies. They are labels. The only thing that *reads* them is a filter — and a tag nobody can filter by is decoration, so this slice has one.

**Filtering — SETTLE THIS.** Recommendation: the cards' filter panel gains a **Tag** category, a union within the category and AND with the rest, reusing `matchesFilters`, counting as one active filter like every other category, and staying view state (never persisted; the saved-preset system is card filters and stays that way). For the initiatives flow, filtering follows the control task 76 adds — the same control growing a tag axis, or its own — and is the part to settle when that lands. Either way counts read the column: narrowing what you see never changes the load a column carries.

Where it surfaces: chips on the card face for cards and initiatives alike, beside the type chip (and beside task 76's kind chip, if that lands first), capped with a "+N" rather than wrapping a narrow card in a wall of chips; the item panel, as an add/remove control; board settings, as a section to add, rename, recolour and remove — next to the initiative-kind section and clearly distinct from the card-type *default* picker, whose label already overstates what it does; and both CSV exports gain a Tag column (the board's cards and the dashboard's initiatives), joined with semicolons the way assignees are, so a comma in a tag name cannot break the column.

Persistence: both fields are optional, so old state reads as no tags and no list — **no version bump and no migrate**. Export/import carries boards and items wholesale, so `WORKSPACE_KEYS` is unchanged. `duplicateBoard` copies a board's tags with the rest of its design; a `BoardTemplate` does **not** carry them, because a template designs a flow and v27 settled that it is not a vocabulary.

Non-goals: no workspace-wide tag registry and no sharing between boards; no nested or hierarchical tags; no tag-level permissions; no automatic or suggested tagging; no counts, analytics or reports per tag — that is a metrics feature and metrics are out of scope for now; and no effect on anything a card's status is derived from.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit-test applying and removing several tags on a card and on an initiative; the same tag twice is refused; a tag from another board cannot be applied; removing a tag in use is refused and says how many carry it; a tag renamed or recoloured shows the new name everywhere at once, with nothing copied onto the items; and a dangling tag id renders nothing rather than an id (delete the board that defined it). **Parity as a test**: rollup bucket, lane counts, health flags, dependency state and flow numbers are identical with and without tags. **Filtering**: the Tag category narrows to cards carrying any selected tag (union within, AND with the rest), counts as one active filter, is not persisted and is not a saved preset, and does not move a lane's count. Persistence: a board with tags, and items carrying them, round-trip through `persistedSlice` / `migrateState`; an old board without the field loads with none; `duplicateBoard` carries the list and `templateFromBoard` does not. Over CDP: add two tags to a card and one to an initiative and see the chips on both faces and in the panels; filter the board by one and watch the cards narrow while the counts stay; rename a tag in board settings and watch every chip change; confirm a refused removal says how many still carry it. Run `npm test` and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: The panel offered OKRs on an initiative that cannot carry them
tasks.description: A team board's initiative showed the "Map an OKR" checkboxes, and every one of them did nothing: the model accepts attribution on strategic initiatives only.
tasks.details:
Reported from the side drawer: the app shows OKRs but does not let you connect an initiative to one. It was the panel lying, not the model failing.

`setAttribution` refuses `on` unless `isStrategicInitiative(itemId)` — an Initiative placed on a portfolio-band board — because everything below inherits through the decomposition, and the model has a test for it (a card, a team initiative and a value-stream initiative are all refused; a strategic one is allowed). The panel, though, gated the whole "Strategic impact" section on `isInitiative` alone, so on any team board it rendered the checkboxes and a silent refusal behind each one. That is the one failure the house rules are most against: a control that appears to work and quietly does not.

Fix: offer the mapping only where the model accepts it. A strategic initiative keeps the section as it was; a non-strategic one shows the same panel with the reason instead of the control — "OKRs attach to strategic initiatives … this one inherits the OKRs it serves from the strategic initiative above it" — and still lists any attribution it carries, with its unlink, since removing is always allowed and a stale mapping has to be clearable.

The neighbour was checked for the same flaw: `linkTeamInitiative` creates a team initiative beneath whatever it is called on and does exactly that, so it is not inert.
tasks.testStrategy: The model already has its test (`OKRs attach to strategic initiatives only`), so this is a UI fix verified in the browser: on a team board (Team Atlas), open an initiative's panel and confirm the OKR section explains the rule and offers no checkboxes; on a portfolio board (Company Strategy), open a strategic initiative and confirm the checkboxes are there and that checking one writes an attribution edge. Run npm test and the dependency scan.

tasks.title: The panel's tag picker is a field you type into, not a list you read
tasks.description: The Tags field offered a select of the board's tags. It is now a text field with the board's vocabulary under it, filtered as you type.
tasks.details:
Requested: \"the tags field should be a text field that offers a drop down of existing tags on "
\"that board and some auto-complete\".\n\n"
A select made you read a list to find a word you already knew. `TagInput` (new component) replaces "
it: focus the field and the board's tags are there, swatch and all; type and it narrows, prefixes "
first (\"de\" reaches Debt before Tech-debt); ArrowUp/ArrowDown move the highlight, Enter takes it, "
a click takes it too and leaves the caret in the field so the next tag is another word. It carries "
the combobox roles (aria-expanded/controls/autocomplete, aria-activedescendant, listbox/option) so "
the keyboard and screen-reader pass still holds.\n\n"
It offers the tags the board **defines** and no others. A tag is this board's managed vocabulary "
with a colour that has to mean something; a word nobody defined is not one, so the field says "
where to define it (board settings) rather than inventing a colour for it. That is the same stance "
as the model's `toggleItemTag`, which refuses an id the board does not list.\n\n"
Empty is never blank: the board defines nothing; every tag it defines is already on the item; the "
typed word is already on the item; or nothing matches and here is where tags are defined.\n\n"
One thing the browser turned up: Escape in the field closed the whole drawer, because App's global "
Escape handler walks the layer stack and knew nothing about this list. A popover is dismissed "
first, as the card menu's flyout is, so the open list now swallows the key and a second Escape "
closes the panel.
tasks.testStrategy:
Verified in the browser on Team Atlas (which defines security, tech-debt, customer-facing) and on "
Company Strategy (which defines none): focus lists all three; typing \"te\" narrows to tech-debt and "
Enter adds it; a click adds one and keeps the caret in the field; typing a carried tag says \"Already "
on this item.\"; typing nonsense points at board settings; an item wearing all of them says so; a "
board with no tags says so; ArrowDown moves the highlight; Escape closes the list and leaves the "
panel, and a second Escape closes the panel. npm test, build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: A tag nobody defined yet can be created from the item that wants it
tasks.description: The Tags field offers to create a word the board does not define, and applying it is one gesture — the tag is the board's from then on, managed in board settings like any other.
tasks.details:
Asked for after 84: let the user create tags on the fly from the Tags field.\n\n"
The field now ends its list with `Create “x”` when the typed word is one the board has never "
heard. Enter (or a click) defines the tag on the board and applies it to the item in one "
gesture. Board settings stays where tags are *managed* — renamed, recoloured, removed — and "
the created tag arrives there like any other.\n\n"
`addTag` now returns the new tag's id so the caller can use the tag it has just defined: two "
facts in the model (the board's vocabulary, the item's set), one gesture in the panel. "
`toggleItemTag`'s guard still runs, so nothing is applied that the board does not list.\n\n"
The one thing it will not do is make a second tag differing only in case: a name the board "
already defines — carried on this item or not — *is* that tag, and the list offers it instead "
of a create row.\n\n"
A new tag needs a colour, and somebody mid-thought should not have to pick one; but every "
created tag the same grey would make the board's vocabulary unreadable, which is the one thing "
a tag is for. So `TAG_PALETTE` cycles — a default, not a decision, and board settings recolours "
any of them. The create row's tooltip says so.
tasks.testStrategy:
A store test: `addTag` hands back the id, the tag is on the board, `toggleItemTag` accepts it "
and the item carries it; the created tag is then an ordinary one (renamed, refused removal in "
use) and a blank name creates nothing. In the browser on Team Atlas: typing \"compliance\" "
offers `Create “compliance”`, Enter applies it and the board defines it in the palette's next "
colour; typing a name the board already defines offers the tag rather than a second one. "
npm test, build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: The card's hover kebab is gone; the menu keeps its other doors
tasks.description: Asked for: remove the kebab menu icon from the top right of cards on hover.
tasks.details:
The narrow card drew a `MoreHorizontal` button in its header row, revealed on hover, wired to "
`openCardMenu`. It is removed, and with it the import.\n\n"
The card menu is unchanged and still reachable three ways: right-click (on the card root), "
Shift+F10 or the ContextMenu key on a focused card (`cardKeyboard`), and — for touch — the item "
panel, which carries the same actions. The `onContextMenu` prop stays exactly as it was, so "
nothing else moved.\n\n"
What this does give up: on a coarse pointer the button was the one always-visible door to the "
menu (`pointer-coarse:opacity-100`), and there is no long-press. Tap → panel is the touch path "
now. A long-press could be added to `useCardLift` if the menu is wanted there.
tasks.testStrategy:
Verified in the browser: no element with `aria-label=\"Card actions\"` remains on the board; "
right-click still opens the card menu, and Shift+F10 on a focused card still opens it. npm "
test, build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: Everywhere the app can be is a URL: board, card, view
tasks.description: Asked for: a unique URL for each board, each initiative or card on it, and each view of it. The app now writes the URL as well as reading it, and follows the back button.
tasks.details:
Before this the app read about fifteen query parameters on boot and never wrote one: no shareable link, no back button. Now the URL is the app's own state, in both directions.

**The place** is three facts and one canonical query — `/?board=b-atlas`, `/?board=b-atlas&view=timeline`, `/?board=b-atlas&item=init-signup`, or both at once. `lib/url.ts` is the pure mapping (`viewOf`, `urlQuery`, `placeFromQuery`); `lib/useUrl.ts` is the one owner of the URL, reading on the way in and writing on the way out, with a `popstate` listener for the back button.

**Canonical, not merely faithful**: the query is rebuilt from the state every time and anything unrecognised is dropped, so one place has exactly one URL and two people looking at the same thing hold the same link. The other parameters are *intentions* — read once on arrival and normalised away (`?q=`, `?filters=`, `?collapse=`, `?select=`, `?lens=`, `?boundary=`, `?stress=`, `?edit=`).

**History**: a board and a view are journeys, so each is a step the back button undoes; an open card is the same place with something drawn over it, so it rewrites the step it is on. The alternative — a step per card — leaves a duplicate behind on every dismissal, and back then looks broken once before it works.

**Three decisions worth recording.** `?edit=` is an intention, not a place: edit mode is a mode, and the back button must never be the thing that throws a board design away. `viewOf`'s order matches App's render order, so a state that somehow held two flags still resolves to the view on screen. And a link naming a board or a card that is not here — from another dataset, or to something since deleted — lands on what is there rather than on a blank surface under a URL claiming otherwise.

**Also**: the store gained `setView`, the one name-driven door for all seven views, delegating to the existing tab setters so the rules about which view clears what live in one place; the TopBar's tabs now go through it too, so a tab and a link mean the same thing. `?view=mywork` and `?view=boards` — which the old boot parser did not know — now work. The README's deep-link list, which named boards from two datasets ago, is replaced by the scheme itself.

One bug found by reviewing rather than by probing: an absent `view` was read as "no opinion" when it is written as "the board's own flow", so the back button out of the Timeline left the screen on the Timeline under a URL that no longer mentioned it. The two directions now agree, and that is tested.
tasks.testStrategy: 13 new tests in `lib/url.test.ts`: every view named from its flags, precedence, the canonical query per place, one URL per place and no two places sharing one, the round trip, the legacy `view=metrics`, unknown names, and a hand-written link normalising to the same place. Plus a store test that `setView` and `viewOf` agree for all eight names and that exactly one flag is ever set.\n\nVerified in a fresh browser tab (so history starts clean): a first visit normalises to `?board=b-portfolio`; switching board through the picker writes `?board=b-atlas` and adds a step; opening a card writes `?board=…&item=…` without adding one; dismissing it drops the item with no duplicate; the Timeline tab writes `?board=…&view=timeline`, back returns to the Board view, forward returns to the Timeline; all six views load from a URL; a link naming a board and a card that are gone lands on a real board with no panel; and `?board=b-atlas&item=init-trial&q=trial&edit=1` opens the card, narrows the board, starts editing, and normalises the URL to `?board=b-atlas&item=init-trial`. npm test, build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: Type and Kind are properties in Details, and Kind joins the context menu
tasks.description: Asked for: move initiative kind and card type out of the panel's ⋮ menu into the Details tab, and add Kind to the context menu for initiatives.
tasks.details:
Both controls sat behind the panel's ⋮ menu, which made a property look like an action — you could not read an item's type or kind without opening a menu. They are now cells in the Details property grid, beside Status, Priority, Lead and the rest: **Type** for a card (the card types only, so nothing becomes an initiative), **Kind** for an initiative.

An initiative shows no Type cell and does not need one: the type is what makes it an initiative, it is fixed, and the header already wears the chip. What stays in the ⋮ menu is the note about *why* — a menu is where you would look for the missing control, so the missing affordance still explains itself. A card's ⋮ menu is now purely actions (Duplicate, Archive, Delete); the button's tooltip no longer promises a card type it does not have.

The context menu gained **Kind** for initiatives, next to where a card's Type sits. It is offered only when the *whole* selection is initiatives — the exact mirror of hiding Type whenever any of it is one, so nothing offered applies to "some of the group". The flyout lists None and the board's kinds with the one worn marked, and a kind defined on another board still appears (tagged "another board"), because the menu must not lie about what the item says.

`setItemsKind` is new: the menu acts on a selection, so the setter does too, refusing a kind no board defines for the whole selection rather than half-applying it, and setting it only on the initiatives in a mixed one. `setInitiativeKind` now delegates to it, so the rule lives in one place.

One thing left as it was: on a board that defines no kinds, the Kind control offers only None. It is a real control with nothing to choose (the Kind *filter* hides itself in that case), and it could hide itself the same way — left visible for now, since it is also how a person discovers that kinds exist.
tasks.testStrategy: A store test for `setItemsKind`: a mixed selection sets the kind on its initiatives and nowhere else, clearing is the same gesture, and an id no board defines is refused for the whole selection. Verified in the browser: a card's Details reads Type (User Story|Epic|Bug|Spike|Task) with no Kind, and its context menu has Type and no Kind; an initiative's Details reads Kind with no Type, its ⋮ menu still carries the \"type is fixed\" note, and its context menu has Kind and no Type; on the Growth value stream the Kind flyout reads None | Workstream | Enabler with the worn one checked, and picking Enabler wrote it to the item. npm test, build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: The initiative card leads with its kind, its title and what is under it
tasks.description: Asked for: kinds identifiable at a glance by colour, an initiative shape clearly different from a card, and the focus on the title, the kind and the children's statuses — with the issue codes demoted.
tasks.details:
The wide card was a card with more on it. It is now a different shape.

**The kind is a band across the top**, in the kind's own colour, with the picker behind it. A card is tinted by its type and railed down the left; an initiative wears its kind as a band — so the two are told apart before either is read, and a reader can see what sort of initiative it is without reading a word of the title. `KindChip` became `KindBand`, and it now takes an optional kind and an optional `onSet`, so it can render the empty slot too.

**When the band shows**: whenever the item wears a kind, or the board defines any. A board that defines none shows no band — there is nothing to say and nothing to choose, the same rule the Kind filter keeps. A board that defines some shows the band even on an initiative wearing none, reading "No kind" and offering the board's kinds: the empty slot is how a person discovers that kinds exist, and it is the slot they click to fill. In edit mode the band stays and stops being a control — the previous chip vanished there, which lost the initiative's identity exactly when the board was being designed.

**The reading order is now the priority order**: the band, then the title at `text-title` (15px — the largest text on the board) with priority and the reference beside it, then the children's own stages as 12px pips sorted into the columns' order, with the counts (`N below`, `N open`) and the rollup percentage, then a full-width progress bar, then the warnings, then everything quiet — lineage, tags, links, checklist, size, people. The pips carry a tooltip naming each child and its stage, and the row's own tooltip sums the spread ("7 directly below: 3 done, 2 in progress, 2 not started").

**The reference is demoted**, not removed: `INIT12` is how an initiative is *named* in a standup, not how it is read, so it is 11px, grey, right-aligned and out of the reading path. The size moved to the quiet footer, and the old `Layers N` icon went — the pips say it better.

**One contradiction the redesign exposed and fixed**: the pips were built from the children *excluding* archived ones, while `childCount` and the rollup counted all of them — so an initiative whose only child had been filed away read "nothing below" and "1 below" at once. The pips now cover the same set the rollup does, which is the domain rule the tests already state (`archived leaves still count toward rollup but not toward open pressure`).

Also fixed while in there: the kind picker had no keydown handler, so Escape with its list open bubbled to App and closed the whole panel — the same bug the tag field had.
tasks.testStrategy: No component tests exist (the vitest environment is node), so this is verified in the browser. On the Growth value stream (which defines Workstream and Enabler): the band reads WORKSTREAM in the kind's colour with white text; a new initiative's band reads NO KIND in neutral slate and lists None | Workstream | Enabler when clicked; picking Enabler turns the band slate, retitles it ENABLER and writes `kind-b-portfolio-enabler` to the item; Escape closes the list rather than the board. On Team Atlas (which defines no kinds) there is no band, and the shape still reads as an initiative: 15px title, status pips, full-width bar, quiet footer — beside the cards workflow's small tinted notes with their type chip and left rail. `npm test` (312), build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: One badge set for every warning, in one place, and bigger child indicators
tasks.description: Asked for: larger initiative child indicators, and blocked / uncommitted / other warnings as a consistently positioned set of badges.
tasks.details:
**The child indicators are 16px** (were 12), with a 4px radius, still sorted into the columns' order and still capped at twelve with a `+N`.

**The warnings are now one set of badges in one place**: a row between the progress bar and the quiet footer, so a reader scanning a column knows where to look and a card with nothing to say says nothing. The set is `initiativeHealth`'s own flags — the same rules, the same words and the same tones the dashboard's Health column reads, so an initiative cannot be at risk in one place and quiet in another.

**One shape, two weights.** Every badge is the same size, radius and type scale; the tone carries the domain's own distinction. A hard stop is solid (`bg-rose-600`, bold) — the card has always drawn a blockage that way, "so a blockage anywhere beneath it reads at a glance rather than as another piece of metadata" — and something to watch is pale, ringed and lighter in weight, so a card carrying four watches does not shout the way a card carrying a blockage does. The words and the titles are the domain's: a badge never invents its own vocabulary.

**Two exceptions the card owns**, both commented at the site: "nothing below" is not repeated as a badge because the children row already says it where the pips would be; and a blockage rolled up from team cards keeps the softer tone and the "blocked below" wording the card has always given it, so a programme reader is not shouted at with a fact three levels down. "Waiting on" moved out of the footer into the set: it is the one warning the health rules do not own, because it is about the item itself rather than the work below it. The dependents signal joined the set too, in the same shape and tone as the other watches.

**Cost, measured, because health is the one derivation on this surface that is not linear in the size of the board** — the waiting rule walks the links once per open descendant and the staleness rule looks up a placement for each of them. On `?stress=300` (298 cards, nine initiatives) it is worth about 33ms per change to the work.
