So it is computed once per change to the work rather than once per render, in a `useMemo` keyed on the store's own arrays plus the day (one rule counts days, and a board left open overnight must not go on saying "still 12d"). Measured A/B against the previous commit: a selection on the stress board costs 118.5ms before and 114-122ms after — the memo holds, and the interactive path pays nothing. The residual is a domain-side characteristic the dashboard has always had (O(open × links)); a links-by-endpoint index in `derive` would fix it for both surfaces, and is not done here.
tasks.testStrategy: No component tests exist (the vitest environment is node), so this is verified in the browser. On the Growth value stream: `1 blocked below` renders pale with the softened wording on the board's own flow while `1 blocked` renders solid in the Linked boards band beneath it; `1 waiting` is solid and `still 7d` / `21 pts below` / `2 backlog` / `1 due later` are pale; all of them sit in one row under the bar. On Team Atlas the pips are visibly larger, and the cards workflow's narrow cards are unchanged. `npm test` (312), build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: An initiative's drawer opens with its warnings, and the cards they are about
tasks.description: Asked for: clicking an initiative that has warnings should open the drawer with a warnings section listing the issues and taking you to the relevant cards and board.
tasks.details:
The Details tab — which is what the drawer opens on — now leads with a **Warnings** section, for an initiative that has any. Each warning is its badge (the same shape and the same two weights the card's row uses), the rule's own words beside it, and **the cards the rule found** as rows: a type dot, the reference, the title, the board when it is not the one you are looking at, and an arrow. Clicking a row takes you to that board, the board's own view, and that card's drawer — the order matters, because choosing a board clears the selection by design, so the drawer is opened after it. Up to four cards are named, then the rest are counted.

**The rules now name their members.** `HealthFlagInfo` gained `items`, and `blockedBelow` was split into `blockedBelowItems` with the count as its length, so a badge and the cards it points at cannot drift. The flags about the *shape* of the whole (`stale`, `oversized`) and the one about there being none (`unplanned`) name no cards, with a comment saying why: listing the entire work below under "nothing has moved" would be a list of everything, which is not navigation. The `uncommitted` rule now takes its list from `leafItems` rather than its count from `uncommittedBelow` — the same leaves `rollupOf` counted — so the badge can point at them.

The dependents signal joins the set, as it does on the card: it is a fact about this item rather than a health rule, and the card already draws it as one of the same badges.

An **Open on the board** action appears only when there is somewhere to go — a view that is not the board, or an item that lives on another board — so it is never a control that does nothing.

Health is memoized on the store's own arrays plus the day, for the same reason the board memoizes it: it is the one derivation here that is not linear in the size of the initiative, and a drawer that recomputed it on every keystroke in the description field would stutter.

The badge grammar moved to `lib/colors` (`FLAG_BADGE_SHAPE` / `FLAG_BADGE`) so the card's row and the drawer's section are visibly one set rather than two lookalikes. Two grammar bugs the new section made visible were fixed: "1 card below wait on work" and "1 item depend on this".
tasks.testStrategy: Two new domain tests: each flag's `items` is exactly the cards the rule counted and the number in the label is that list's length; and the shape-of-the-whole and nothing-below rules name no cards. In the browser, on Billing migration (six warnings): the drawer opens on Details with the section, each warning carrying its cards; clicking \"Retire the legacy coupon service\" lands on `?board=b-atlas&item=st-coupon-retire` with that card's drawer open and the initiative in its lineage. On the Growth value stream's own Onboarding journey, whose backlog cards live on Team Atlas, the rows name the board and clicking one lands on `?board=b-atlas&item=init-trial`. From the Timeline, the section offers \"Go to Team Atlas with this initiative open\" and it does. `npm test` (314), build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: Objectives are reachable, readable, and can be made where they are read
tasks.description: Three reports: the OKR page had no way in but a portfolio board's corner; its dark header was hard to read and did not say what to do; and a portfolio offered no way to add an objective.
tasks.details:
**A way in, in the navigation.** `Objectives` is now a tab beside Archive and My work — it is organisation-level, not any one board's, so it sits with the other organisation-level views. It goes through `setView`, so it is addressable like everything else: clicking it lands on `?board=b-atlas&view=objectives`, which is a link somebody can send. The Boards workspace hides the nav (it always has), so the workspace carries its own block — *Objectives & Key Results · N objectives · M key results — what the work is for, and the strategic initiatives that serve it* — above the board grid.

**A header that can be read.** The page's header was a dark strip: `text-slate-600` on `bg-slate-800`, which is **1.9:1** against this app's own 4.5 floor — the legibility rule it tests for in `lib/legibility.test.ts`. It is now the light, tinted panel the other views use (Archive's amber, Boards' indigo, this one violet): an eyebrow, a heading that says how many objectives this period and whether that is over the commitment limit, and a line saying what the page is for. The primary action is a named button — *New objective* — beside the period it will land in, instead of a bare `Objective` at the far end of a dark bar. A new test pins the pairs (and the old strip, as the reason it went).

**Making one where it is read.** The strategy map now has the same control: name an objective in the header and it is created in the latest period the map already shows, arriving as a card with its coverage gap inline — *No strategic initiative serves this OKR* — and the *Map a strategic initiative* control right there, which is the next thing to fix. The empty state no longer sends you to another page to do it.

The objectives button in the strategy map's section header stays: it goes to the *editing* view (period, key results, scores), which is a different errand from making one.
tasks.testStrategy: A new legibility test: the header's three pairs clear the floor on violet-50, and slate-600 on slate-800 does not — the measurement that made the case. In the browser: the nav's Objectives button lands on `?board=b-atlas&view=objectives`; the workspace block reads its counts and lands on the same place; the header reads 3 of 5 this period with the explanation line legible; naming an objective on the page creates it (3 → 4, and the heading follows); and on Company Strategy, naming one in the map creates it (4 → 5) as a card reading \"No strategic initiative serves this OKR\" with its map control. `npm test` (315), build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: A portfolio reads its objectives through its own initiative workflow
tasks.description: Asked for: users connect OKRs to initiatives, and the initiatives appear under that objective in a consistent initiative workflow — the connection and the progress read together.
tasks.details:
The strategy map used to list each objective with its serving initiatives as compact rows: ref, title, kind chip, health chip, percent, stage chip. That said everything and showed nothing — the stage was a chip rather than the column it is everywhere else, and the map was a report *about* the flow rather than the flow.

Now each objective heads **its own initiatives workflow**: this board's own typed columns, the same ones a team board shows, narrowed to the strategic initiatives attributed to it. The initiative sits in the column its own work puts it in, wearing the same card it wears everywhere — kind band, title, children pips, rollup, warnings — so the connection and the progress are read in one place, in the language the rest of the app already speaks.

**The mechanism is one prop.** `BoardSummary` gained `onlyIds`, and everything downstream follows from that single narrowing: a cell's badge counts the group's initiatives, and the health is found for them alone. That last part matters — the health rules are not linear in the size of a board (the waiting rule walks the links once per open descendant), and N groups must not each pay for the whole board. The memo is keyed on the ids as one string, because whoever passes the array rebuilds it every render.

**One objective per row.** The first cut kept the three-across grid and gave every column a twelfth of the page — narrower than the card it had to hold, so titles broke mid-word and the column names truncated. A flow needs the width; the groups stack.

**The gaps stay first-class.** An objective nobody serves says so in words instead of drawing four empty boxes — 'nothing yet' and 'served from somewhere else' are different facts and neither is a workflow. An initiative serving no objective gets a flow of its own at the end, with the instruction that maps it: 'map one from the objective it belongs to', which is the direction the per-objective *Map a strategic initiative…* control already works in.

**The flow here is read-only, deliberately.** An initiative may serve several objectives — attribution is a relation, not a container — so the same card can appear in more than one flow, and a lift/drop would not know which group it was rearranging. Making it draggable means answering that first.

Also fixed, found by clicking around in it: a **read-only kind band swallowed the click** — it stopped propagation before checking whether it was a control, so on a surface that only reads another board's flow, clicking the band did nothing instead of opening the card.

AGENTS.md and the README said the map 'replaces the initiatives workflow'; both now say it *is* the workflow, grouped by what the work is for.

tasks.title: A portfolio shows its objectives and nothing else
tasks.description: Asked for: no Linked boards on portfolio boards — just the objectives, their key results, and the initiatives attributed to them in their grouped flows.
tasks.details:
The Linked boards section — and the line under it explaining what a band is — now renders on a **program** board only. A portfolio's surface is its strategy map and nothing else, which is the reading it exists for: what the work is *for*, and the initiatives that serve it, grouped by the objective they answer to.

The links themselves stay in the model, so this is a decision about one surface and not about the data — a programme under a portfolio still rolls up. They are still manageable: **Board settings** has carried the linked-boards list for every aggregating board all along, and a portfolio now says there why its own surface will not show them: "A portfolio shows no bands: these roll up on the programme boards beneath it." Said where the link is made, because that is where somebody would otherwise wonder why nothing happened.

One correctness fix alongside it, in the spirit of the ask: an objective's flow now holds **any** of the board's initiatives attributed to it, not only the local top-level ones. `serving()` read from `mine` — which exists to keep a nested initiative from being a second row the map *heads* — but the OKR page will happily attribute a nested one, and then it belonged in that objective's flow and was missing from it. Coverage still reads `mine`: an outcome is committed or it is not, and a piece of one is not a separate commitment.

tasks.title: A board that renders no cards workflow does not make cards
tasks.description: Asked for: remove the + Card button from a portfolio board.
tasks.details:
The toolbar's **Card** button and the palette's **New card** verb are now offered only on a board that renders a cards workflow. Both asked the domain the same question — `isAggregating` — so the two ways in cannot disagree, the same way `isBoardSurface` already answers the toolbar and the side panels.

It is stated as that rule rather than as "not on a portfolio" because a **programme** board has the same property: it shows the initiatives workflow and its linked bands, and no cards workflow either, so a card made there was equally one nobody could see on the board that made it. If a programme board should keep the button, it is one line.

**Initiative stays on both.** It is what a coordination board is read for: on a portfolio the new initiative arrives in the strategy map with its coverage gap, waiting for an objective to carry it — which is the flow the map was built around.

The card still exists as a model fact on such a board (the store will take one, and it reads in My work, the Archive and the Flow metrics) — this is the UI declining to offer something it cannot show, not the model refusing it.
tasks.testStrategy: In the browser, per band: a **portfolio** offers `Initiative` alone in the toolbar and `New initiative` alone in the palette; a **programme** the same; a **team** board offers both, in both places. `npm test` (315), build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.

tasks.title: An initiative serves one objective
tasks.description: Reported: the same strategic initiative could be mapped to several OKRs. Restricted to one.
tasks.details:
Attribution was a relation — many initiatives to many objectives — and the app made a feature of it ("Serves 2 OKRs — still 1 unit of WIP"). It is now **one objective per initiative**, and the shape is the one the rest of the model already uses for a single choice: **choosing again moves it**, the way `setParent` moves a card and a kind replaces a kind. Nothing accumulates, nothing is refused — the choice replaces the choice.

`setAttribution` is the one door and keeps the rule: mapping to an objective the initiative already serves changes nothing (rather than adding a second edge), mapping to a new one drops whatever it served before, and unmapping leaves it serving none.

**Persistence version 31**, with a migration: state from before the rule keeps the first objective each initiative was mapped to and drops the rest. The same reasoning as v12, which dropped attributions pointing at non-initiatives — an edge the model would refuse is not an edge. Without the bump the normalisation would never run, because zustand only calls `migrate` when the stored version differs.

**The panel's control became a choice.** It was a list of checkboxes under "Map an OKR" — a multi-select, which is what the model no longer is, so the control would have been lying about it. It is now the select the kind and the type use, reading "No OKR" or the objective it serves, with that objective's key results under it. The "Serves N OKRs" line is gone with the rule it described.

**Both mapping selects say when a choice will move something**: an initiative that already serves another objective is offered as "… — moves from <objective>", so the move is visible before it happens rather than discovered afterwards.

The README's "What to try" bullet made the old rule its example ("serves 2 objectives; WIP stays 1") and now says what happens instead.
tasks.testStrategy: Two new tests. Store: mapping to a second objective moves it (one edge, the first gone), choosing what it already serves changes nothing, and clearing leaves none. Migration: state carrying two attributions for one initiative keeps the first and drops the second, while other edges are untouched. In the browser: the map's select offers \"INIT1 Recurring revenue engine — moves from Grow activation\"; mapping it left Grow activation at 0 serving with its coverage note and the gap count at 3, and put it in Reduce cost to serve at 2 serving, in its column; the drawer's control is a select reading \"Reduce cost to serve · FY26 Q4\", and choosing Grow activation moved it back, one attribution per initiative throughout. `npm test` (317), build, lint and the dependency scan are clean.
